The Nonlinearity Index
CatalogUse casesAboutStar on GitHub

A catalogue of activation functions

y = φ(Wx + b)

Everything a neural network can learn beyond a straight line comes from φ, the activation function.

This index collects them: the formula, how the curve behaves, and a plot of it and its derivative. It's organised by family, from the classics every framework ships to learned and experimental functions from the research literature. A use-case guide explains which ones get picked for which jobs, and why.

374 of ≈400 functions catalogued · 18 families · 3 tiers

I

Classic

The functions every framework ships: sigmoidal curves, rectifiers, thresholds and the output layers built on them.

39 functions

Linear & threshold

3

The simplest maps: pass the input through, or snap it to a few discrete values.

Identity

Linear

f(x) = x

Passes the input through unchanged. It's the right output for regression and appears inside residual paths. A network built only from identity activations collapses into a single linear map.

  • (−∞, ∞)
  • smooth
  • monotonic
  • torch.nn.Identity

Chosen for Financial and noisy time-series forecasting, Reinforcement learning policies and value functions, Output layers: matching the target

Binary step

Heaviside

f(x) =1if x ≥ 00if x < 0

Fires 1 or 0, like the original perceptron. Its derivative is zero almost everywhere, so plain gradient descent can't train it; spiking and binary networks use surrogate gradients instead.

  • {0, 1}
  • non-smooth
  • monotonic
  • bounded

Rosenblatt, 1958

Chosen for Binary and spiking neural networks

Sign

Signum

f(x) = sign(x)

Binarises activations to ±1. Binary neural networks use it in the forward pass so multiplications become bit operations, and train through it with a straight-through estimator.

  • {−1, 0, 1}
  • non-smooth
  • monotonic
  • bounded

Courbariaux et al., 2016 (BinaryNet)

Chosen for Binary and spiking neural networks

Sigmoidal & saturating

13

S-shaped curves that squash the real line into a bounded interval. Their gradients vanish once they saturate.

Sigmoid

Logistic

σ(x) = 1 / (1 + e−x)

Squashes any input into (0, 1), so it reads as a probability. It saturates for large |x| and its gradient peaks at 0.25, which made deep sigmoid networks hard to train. Still the standard choice for binary outputs and LSTM/GRU gates.

  • (0, 1)
  • smooth
  • monotonic
  • bounded
  • torch.nn.Sigmoid

Chosen for Medical image segmentation, Recurrent networks (LSTM, GRU), Output layers: matching the target

Tanh

Hyperbolic tangent

tanh(x) = (ex − e−x) / (ex + e−x)

A rescaled sigmoid (tanh x = 2σ(2x) − 1) that is zero-centred but saturating: its gradient peaks at 1 at x = 0 and vanishes for large |x|. Used for the LSTM/GRU candidate state, PPO hidden layers, GAN generator outputs and physics-informed networks.

  • (−1, 1)
  • smooth
  • monotonic
  • bounded
  • torch.nn.Tanh

LeCun et al., 1998 (Efficient BackProp)

Chosen for Financial and noisy time-series forecasting, Recurrent networks (LSTM, GRU), Generative adversarial networks, Physics-informed neural networks, Reinforcement learning policies and value functions, Output layers: matching the target

LeCun tanh

Scaled tanh

f(x) = 1.7159 · tanh(2x / 3)

Tanh rescaled so that f(±1) = ±1, which keeps unit-variance inputs at roughly unit variance and keeps the units away from saturation.

  • (−1.7159, 1.7159)
  • smooth
  • monotonic
  • bounded

LeCun et al., 1998

Arctan

Inverse tangent

f(x) = arctan(x)

Shaped like tanh but approaches its limits polynomially rather than exponentially, so it saturates more gently and keeps a usable gradient further from zero.

  • (−π/2, π/2)
  • smooth
  • monotonic
  • bounded

Softsign

Elliott function

f(x) = x / (1 + |x|)

A tanh-like curve with polynomial tails: it saturates more slowly than tanh, so gradients survive further from the origin. Studied as a tanh replacement in deep feed-forward nets.

  • (−1, 1)
  • smooth
  • monotonic
  • bounded
  • torch.nn.Softsign

Elliott, 1993; Glorot & Bengio, 2010

Hard sigmoid

f(x) =0if x ≤ −3x / 6 + 1/2if −3 < x < 31if x ≥ 3

A piecewise-linear stand-in for the sigmoid. It's cheap and quantisation-friendly, which is why MobileNetV3 uses it in squeeze-and-excitation blocks. Some libraries use a slope of 0.2 instead of 1/6.

  • [0, 1]
  • non-smooth
  • monotonic
  • bounded
  • torch.nn.Hardsigmoid

Chosen for Mobile, edge and quantised inference

Hard tanh

f(x) = max(−1, min(1, x))

Clips to [−1, 1] with slope 1 in between. The gradient is exactly zero outside the linear zone; binary networks use its derivative as the straight-through estimator.

  • [−1, 1]
  • non-smooth
  • monotonic
  • bounded
  • torch.nn.Hardtanh

Chosen for Binary and spiking neural networks

Log-sigmoid

f(x) = log σ(x) = −softplus(−x)

The logarithm of the sigmoid, computed stably. It mostly appears inside losses (binary cross-entropy, word2vec negative sampling) rather than as a hidden-layer activation.

  • (−∞, 0)
  • smooth
  • monotonic
  • torch.nn.LogSigmoid

Error function

erf

erf(x) = (2/√π) ∫0x e−t² dt

The Gauss error function: the normal CDF rescaled to (−1, 1). It behaves like tanh but saturates faster, because its tails are Gaussian.

  • (−1, 1)
  • smooth
  • monotonic
  • bounded

Probit (normal CDF)

Φ, Gaussian CDF

Φ(x) = ½ [1 + erf(x / √2)]

The cumulative distribution of a standard normal. As an output link it gives probit regression; inside a network it's the gate in GELU.

  • (0, 1)
  • smooth
  • monotonic
  • bounded

Complementary log-log

cloglog, Gompertz link

f(x) = 1 − exp(−ex)

An asymmetric sigmoid: it leaves 0 slowly and approaches 1 quickly. It's the natural link for discrete-time survival models with proportional hazards, and for rare-event binary outcomes.

  • (0, 1)
  • smooth
  • monotonic
  • bounded

Chosen for Output layers: matching the target

Gudermannian

gd

gd(x) = 2 arctan(tanh(x / 2))

Connects circular and hyperbolic functions. Another smooth, odd, saturating curve between tanh and arctan in how fast it saturates.

  • (−π/2, π/2)
  • smooth
  • monotonic
  • bounded

ISRU

Inverse square root unit

f(x) = x / √(1 + αx²)

Inverse square root unit: tanh-shaped, but needs only a square root instead of exponentials, which is cheaper on some hardware. α sets the bounds ±1/√α (α = 1 plotted).

  • (−1/√α, 1/√α)
  • smooth
  • monotonic
  • bounded

Carlile et al., 2017

Rectifiers (ReLU family)

13

Identity for positive inputs, something cheaper or flatter for negative ones. The default hidden-layer choice since about 2011.

ReLU

Rectified linear unit

f(x) = max(0, x)

Zero for negative inputs, identity for positive ones. It's cheap, doesn't saturate for x > 0 and produces sparse activations, which made deep networks practical. A unit that only ever sees negative inputs stops learning: a 'dead' ReLU.

  • [0, ∞)
  • non-smooth
  • monotonic
  • torch.nn.ReLU

Nair & Hinton, 2010; Glorot et al., 2011

Chosen for Transformer feed-forward blocks, Image classification CNNs, Medical image segmentation, Mobile, edge and quantised inference, Generative adversarial networks, Implicit neural representations, Graph neural networks, Deep tabular models and deep MLPs, Reinforcement learning policies and value functions, Sparse coding and denoising

Leaky ReLU

LReLU

f(x) =xif x ≥ 0αxif x < 0

Gives negative inputs a small slope α (0.01 by default) so units never fully die. GAN discriminators and graph attention networks typically use α = 0.2.

  • (−∞, ∞)
  • non-smooth
  • monotonic
  • torch.nn.LeakyReLU

Maas et al., 2013

Chosen for Image classification CNNs, Medical image segmentation, Generative adversarial networks, Graph neural networks, Audio and waveform generation

RReLU

Randomised leaky ReLU

f(x) =xif x ≥ 0ax, a ~ U(1/8, 1/3) in trainingif x < 0

A leaky ReLU whose negative slope is sampled at random during training, which adds a little regularising noise. At test time the slope is fixed to the mean, (l + u)/2 ≈ 0.23, which is what's plotted.

  • (−∞, ∞)
  • non-smooth
  • monotonic
  • torch.nn.RReLU

Xu et al., 2015

ReLU6

f(x) = min(max(0, x), 6)

ReLU capped at 6. The bounded range keeps activations representable in low-precision fixed-point arithmetic, which is why mobile networks such as MobileNetV2 adopted it.

  • [0, 6]
  • non-smooth
  • monotonic
  • bounded
  • torch.nn.ReLU6

Krizhevsky, 2010; Howard et al., 2017

Chosen for Mobile, edge and quantised inference

Thresholded ReLU

f(x) =xif x > θ0otherwise

Passes values only above a threshold θ (θ = 1 plotted). It was introduced for zero-bias autoencoders, where it gives sparse codes without learned biases.

  • {0} ∪ (θ, ∞)
  • non-smooth
  • monotonic
  • torch.nn.Threshold

Konda et al., 2015

Absolute value

Abs rectification

f(x) = |x|

Rectifies both signs, so it discards the sign but keeps the magnitude. Early multi-stage vision systems used absolute-value rectification of filter responses.

  • [0, ∞)
  • non-smooth
  • non-monotonic

Jarrett et al., 2009

CReLU

Concatenated ReLU

f(x) = [ReLU(x), ReLU(−x)]

Concatenates ReLU(x) and ReLU(−x), doubling the channels so no information is thrown away. It was motivated by the observation that early CNN filters tend to learn negated pairs.

  • [0, ∞)²
  • non-smooth
  • non-monotonic

Shang et al., 2016

Softplus

f(x) = ln(1 + ex)

A smooth ReLU: always positive and differentiable everywhere. Common as an output for quantities that must be positive (variances, rates), and the inner function of Mish.

  • (0, ∞)
  • smooth
  • monotonic
  • torch.nn.Softplus

Dugas et al., 2001

Chosen for Financial and noisy time-series forecasting, Physics-informed neural networks, Output layers: matching the target

ELU

Exponential linear unit

f(x) =xif x > 0α(ex − 1)if x ≤ 0

Identity for positive inputs and a smooth exponential that saturates at −α for negative ones (α = 1 plotted). The negative outputs push mean activations toward zero, which speeds up learning.

  • (−α, ∞)
  • smooth
  • monotonic
  • torch.nn.ELU

Clevert et al., 2015

Chosen for Financial and noisy time-series forecasting, Graph neural networks

SELU

Scaled ELU

f(x) =λxif x > 0λα(ex − 1)if x ≤ 0

A scaled ELU (λ ≈ 1.0507, α ≈ 1.6733) whose constants make activations converge to zero mean and unit variance across layers, given LeCun-normal initialisation: 'self-normalising' networks that don't need batch norm.

  • (−λα, ∞) ≈ (−1.76, ∞)
  • non-smooth
  • monotonic
  • torch.nn.SELU

Klambauer et al., 2017

Chosen for Deep tabular models and deep MLPs

CELU

Continuously differentiable ELU

f(x) = max(0, x) + min(0, α(ex/α − 1))

A version of ELU that is continuously differentiable for every α. Plain ELU's derivative jumps at 0 whenever α ≠ 1. Plotted for α = 0.5, 1 and 2.

  • (−α, ∞)
  • smooth
  • monotonic
  • torch.nn.CELU

Barron, 2017

ISRLU

Inverse square root linear unit

f(x) =xif x ≥ 0x / √(1 + αx²)if x < 0

ELU-shaped, but the negative side uses an inverse square root instead of an exponential, which is cheaper to compute (α = 1 plotted).

  • (−1/√α, ∞)
  • smooth
  • monotonic

Carlile et al., 2017

Shifted softplus

ssp

f(x) = ln(0.5ex + 0.5)

Softplus shifted down by ln 2 so that f(0) = 0. SchNet uses it so that predicted molecular energies, and the forces derived from them, are smooth.

  • (−ln 2, ∞)
  • smooth
  • monotonic

Schütt et al., 2017 (SchNet)

Chosen for Molecular and materials modelling

Shrinkage & thresholding

3

Functions that zero out small values, borrowed from signal denoising and sparse coding.

Hard shrink

f(x) =xif |x| > λ0otherwise

Zeroes inputs inside [−λ, λ] and passes the rest unchanged (λ = 0.5 plotted). This is hard thresholding, as used in wavelet denoising and sparse coding.

  • {0} ∪ (−∞, −λ) ∪ (λ, ∞)
  • non-smooth
  • monotonic
  • torch.nn.Hardshrink

Chosen for Sparse coding and denoising

Soft shrink

f(x) =x − λif x > λx + λif x < −λ0otherwise

Soft thresholding: zero inside [−λ, λ], and larger values move toward zero by λ. It's the proximal operator of the L1 norm, which is why it appears in unrolled sparse-coding networks such as LISTA.

  • (−∞, ∞)
  • non-smooth
  • monotonic
  • torch.nn.Softshrink

Chosen for Sparse coding and denoising

Tanh shrink

f(x) = x − tanh(x)

What's left after subtracting tanh: almost flat near zero and nearly linear for large |x|. Rarely used in practice, but available in PyTorch.

  • (−∞, ∞)
  • smooth
  • monotonic
  • torch.nn.Tanhshrink

Output & normalising

7

Activations that turn logits into probabilities or positive quantities. Vector functions are plotted for the two-class case.

Softmax

Normalised exponential

softmax(z)i = ezi/T / Σj ezj/T

Turns a vector of logits into a probability distribution. With two classes it reduces to the sigmoid of the logit difference, which is what's plotted against x = z₁ − z₂ for temperatures T = 0.5, 1 and 2. Lower T gives a sharper distribution.

  • (0, 1), sums to 1
  • smooth
  • monotonic
  • bounded
  • torch.nn.Softmax

Chosen for Attention weights, Medical image segmentation, Reinforcement learning policies and value functions, Output layers: matching the target

Log-softmax

f(z)i = zi − log Σj ezj

Log of softmax, computed in one numerically stable step with log-sum-exp. It's paired with negative log-likelihood loss; most cross-entropy implementations use it internally.

  • (−∞, 0)
  • smooth
  • monotonic
  • torch.nn.LogSoftmax

Softmin

softmin(z) = softmax(−z)

Softmax of the negated inputs, so the smallest value gets the most weight. Used for soft nearest-neighbour assignments and differentiable minimums.

  • (0, 1), sums to 1
  • smooth
  • monotonic
  • bounded
  • torch.nn.Softmin

Sparsemax

sparsemax(z) = argminp ∈ Δ ‖p − z‖²

The Euclidean projection of the logits onto the probability simplex. Unlike softmax it can output exact zeros, which gives sparse, more interpretable attention. For two classes it's a hard sigmoid.

  • [0, 1], sums to 1
  • non-smooth
  • monotonic
  • bounded

Martins & Astudillo, 2016

Chosen for Attention weights

1.5-entmax

Entmax

argmaxp ∈ Δ pᵀz + Hα(p), α = 1.5

Sits between softmax (α = 1) and sparsemax (α = 2): smooth near ties, but it can still assign exact zeros. Used for sparse attention in sequence-to-sequence models.

  • [0, 1], sums to 1
  • smooth
  • monotonic
  • bounded

Peters et al., 2019

Chosen for Attention weights

Exponential

f(x) = ex

Maps to strictly positive values. Used as an output for rates and scale parameters (a Poisson intensity, a standard deviation); its unbounded growth makes it unstable in hidden layers.

  • (0, ∞)
  • smooth
  • monotonic
  • torch.exp

Chosen for Output layers: matching the target

Square softmax

SQMAX

f(z)j = (zj + c)² / Σk (zk + c)²

A softmax replacement that uses squares instead of exponentials, with c = 4. Plotted for two classes with z₂ = 0.

  • ≈ [0, 1]
  • smooth
  • non-monotonic
  • bounded

Wuraola et al., 2021 (via Kunc & Kléma, 2024)

II

Modern & learned

Smooth self-gated units, the gated linear units inside today's Transformers, and activations whose shape is learned during training.

155 functions

Smooth self-gated

10

x multiplied by a smooth gate of itself (GELU, SiLU, Mish) and their cheaper approximations.

GELU

Gaussian error linear unit

f(x) = x · Φ(x)

Weights each input by the probability that a standard normal variable falls below it. It's smooth and dips slightly below zero (minimum ≈ −0.17 near x = −0.75). The default in BERT, GPT-2/3 and most Transformers before GLU variants took over.

  • ≈ [−0.17, ∞)
  • smooth
  • non-monotonic
  • torch.nn.GELU

Hendrycks & Gimpel, 2016

Chosen for Transformer feed-forward blocks, Financial and noisy time-series forecasting, Deep tabular models and deep MLPs

GELU (tanh approximation)

f(x) = ½x [1 + tanh(√(2/π) (x + 0.044715x³))]

The fast approximation used in the original BERT and GPT-2 code. It's visually indistinguishable from exact GELU; pick whichever the pretrained weights you load were trained with.

  • ≈ [−0.17, ∞)
  • smooth
  • non-monotonic
  • torch.nn.GELU(approximate='tanh')

Hendrycks & Gimpel, 2016

Chosen for Transformer feed-forward blocks, Diffusion model denoisers

QuickGELU

Sigmoid GELU approximation

f(x) = x · σ(1.702x)

A cheaper sigmoid-based approximation of GELU. OpenAI's CLIP models were trained with it, so loading their weights means using it too.

  • ≈ [−0.16, ∞)
  • smooth
  • non-monotonic

Hendrycks & Gimpel, 2016; Radford et al., 2021 (CLIP)

SiLU / Swish

Swish-1, sigmoid-weighted linear unit

f(x) = x · σ(x)

The input multiplied by its own sigmoid. Smooth and non-monotonic, with a minimum of about −0.28 at x ≈ −1.28. Used in EfficientNet, the YOLO family and most diffusion-model U-Nets.

  • ≈ [−0.28, ∞)
  • smooth
  • non-monotonic
  • torch.nn.SiLU

Elfwing et al., 2017; Ramachandran et al., 2017

Chosen for Image classification CNNs, Financial and noisy time-series forecasting, Diffusion model denoisers, Physics-informed neural networks, Molecular and materials modelling

Hard swish

h-swish

f(x) =0if x ≤ −3x(x + 3) / 6if −3 < x < 3xif x ≥ 3

A piecewise-polynomial approximation of Swish with no exponentials, so it runs fast on mobile CPUs and quantises well. Introduced in MobileNetV3.

  • ≈ [−0.38, ∞)
  • non-smooth
  • non-monotonic
  • torch.nn.Hardswish

Howard et al., 2019

Chosen for Image classification CNNs, Mobile, edge and quantised inference

Mish

f(x) = x · tanh(softplus(x))

Smooth and non-monotonic, unbounded above and bounded below (minimum ≈ −0.31). Very similar to Swish with a slightly deeper negative lobe. Used in the YOLOv4 backbone.

  • ≈ [−0.31, ∞)
  • smooth
  • non-monotonic
  • torch.nn.Mish

Misra, 2019

Chosen for Image classification CNNs

Squareplus

f(x) = (x + √(x² + b)) / 2

An algebraic softplus: no exponentials or logarithms, so it's fast and numerically simple. b controls the curvature near zero (b = 4 plotted).

  • (0, ∞)
  • smooth
  • monotonic

Barron, 2021

SmeLU

Smooth ReLU

f(x) =0if x ≤ −β(x + β)² / 4βif |x| < βxif x ≥ β

Smooth ReLU: replaces ReLU's corner with a quadratic patch of width 2β (β = 1 plotted). Proposed to make recommender-system predictions more reproducible between training runs.

  • [0, ∞)
  • smooth
  • monotonic

Shamir et al., 2020

Squared ReLU

ReLU²

f(x) = max(0, x)²

ReLU squared. Primer's architecture search found it makes Transformer language models train more efficiently, and later efficient-LLM work adopted it.

  • [0, ∞)
  • smooth
  • monotonic

So et al., 2021 (Primer)

Chosen for Transformer feed-forward blocks

StarReLU

f(x) = s · ReLU(x)² + b

Squared ReLU with a learnable scale and bias (initialised to s ≈ 0.894, b ≈ −0.447) that keep the output distribution normalised. Cheaper than GELU with similar accuracy in MetaFormer models.

  • [b, ∞)
  • smooth
  • monotonic

Yu et al., 2022 (MetaFormer baselines)

Gated linear units

6

Two projections, one gating the other. GLU variants are plotted with both halves tied to the same input, i.e. x · g(x).

GLU

Gated linear unit

GLU(a, b) = a ⊗ σ(b)

Splits a projection into a value half a and a gate half b and multiplies a by σ(b), so the network controls how much information flows. Introduced for convolutional language models.

  • (−∞, ∞)
  • smooth
  • non-monotonic
  • torch.nn.GLU

Dauphin et al., 2017

Bilinear

f(a, b) = a ⊗ b

The gate without any nonlinearity: just the elementwise product of two projections. It was surprisingly competitive in Transformer feed-forward experiments, which suggests the multiplication matters more than the exact gate.

  • (−∞, ∞)
  • smooth
  • non-monotonic

Shazeer, 2020

ReGLU

ReGLU(a, b) = a ⊗ ReLU(b)

GLU with a ReLU gate. It beat standard ReLU feed-forward layers at equal compute, and FT-Transformer uses it for tabular data.

  • (−∞, ∞)
  • non-smooth
  • non-monotonic

Shazeer, 2020

Chosen for Deep tabular models and deep MLPs

GEGLU

GEGLU(a, b) = a ⊗ GELU(b)

GLU with a GELU gate. Used in T5 v1.1, Gemma and other Transformer language models.

  • (−∞, ∞)
  • smooth
  • non-monotonic

Shazeer, 2020

Chosen for Transformer feed-forward blocks, Diffusion model denoisers

SwiGLU

SwiGLU(a, b) = a ⊗ SiLU(b) = a ⊗ (b · σ(b))

The feed-forward activation of LLaMA, PaLM, Mistral and most open LLMs. Because it needs three weight matrices instead of two, the hidden size is usually cut to about 2/3 to keep the parameter count equal.

  • (−∞, ∞)
  • smooth
  • non-monotonic

Shazeer, 2020

Chosen for Transformer feed-forward blocks

Gated tanh unit

WaveNet gate, GTU

f(a, b) = tanh(a) ⊗ σ(b)

A bounded tanh 'content' path modulated by a sigmoid gate. The activation inside WaveNet and gated PixelCNN for audio and image generation.

  • (−1, 1)
  • smooth
  • non-monotonic
  • bounded

van den Oord et al., 2016

Chosen for Audio and waveform generation

Learned & adaptive

9

Activations with trainable parameters, so every neuron or channel can learn its own shape. Plots show example parameter values.

PReLU

Parametric ReLU

f(x) =xif x ≥ 0αx, α learnedif x < 0

A leaky ReLU whose negative slope α is learned, usually one per channel and initialised to 0.25. It was used in the first network reported to beat human-level accuracy on ImageNet.

  • (−∞, ∞)
  • non-smooth
  • monotonic
  • torch.nn.PReLU

He et al., 2015

Chosen for Image classification CNNs, Medical image segmentation

Swish-β

Parametric Swish

f(x) = x · σ(βx), β learned

Swish with a trainable β that interpolates between a scaled linear function (β → 0 gives x/2) and ReLU (β → ∞). Plotted for β = 0.5, 1 and 4.

  • (−∞, ∞)
  • smooth
  • non-monotonic

Ramachandran et al., 2017

PELU

Parametric ELU

f(x) =(a / b) xif x ≥ 0a(ex/b − 1)if x < 0

ELU with two learned positive parameters: a sets the saturation level and b the scale. Tying them as a/b keeps the function differentiable at 0. Plotted with a = 1 and b = 0.5, 1, 2.

  • (−a, ∞)
  • smooth
  • monotonic

Trottier et al., 2017

SReLU

S-shaped ReLU

f(x) =tr + ar(x − tr)if x ≥ trxif tl < x < trtl + al(x − tl)if x ≤ tl

Three linear pieces with four learnable parameters (two thresholds, two outer slopes), so it can learn both convex and non-convex shapes. Inspired by psychophysical laws such as Weber–Fechner.

  • (−∞, ∞)
  • non-smooth
  • monotonic

Jin et al., 2016

APL

Adaptive piecewise linear

f(x) = max(0, x) + Σs as max(0, −x + bs)

Adaptive piecewise linear unit: a ReLU plus a sum of learned hinge functions, so each neuron learns its own piecewise-linear shape. Plotted with one hinge (a = 0.5, b = 1).

  • learned
  • non-smooth
  • non-monotonic

Agostinelli et al., 2014

Maxout

f(x) = maxj (wjᵀx + bj)

Outputs the maximum of k learned linear functions, so it can approximate any convex function; ReLU and leaky ReLU are special cases. It costs k times the parameters. Plotted with three example pieces.

  • learned
  • non-smooth
  • non-monotonic

Goodfellow et al., 2013

ACON-C

f(x) = (p₁ − p₂) x · σ(β(p₁ − p₂) x) + p₂x

'Activate or not': a smooth maximum of p₁x and p₂x with learnable p₁, p₂ and switching factor β. With p₁ = 1 and p₂ = 0 it's exactly Swish; Meta-ACON predicts β from the input.

  • learned
  • smooth
  • monotonic

Ma et al., 2021

Padé activation unit

PAU, rational activation

f(x) = P(x) / (1 + |Σk bkxk|)

A learnable rational function (a ratio of polynomials) whose denominator can't reach zero. It can closely approximate standard activations or learn new shapes. Plotted with example coefficients.

  • learned
  • non-smooth
  • non-monotonic

Molina et al., 2020

III

Experimental & research

Periodic and radial functions, the many descendants of Swish and Mish, and other proposals from the literature that are not yet mainstream.

180 functions

Periodic & radial

20

Oscillating and bump-shaped functions used for implicit representations, periodic signals and RBF networks.

Sine (SIREN)

Sinusoid

f(x) = sin(ω₀x)

A periodic activation for coordinate-based networks. With ω₀ = 30 and a matching initialisation, SIRENs represent images, audio and signed distance fields in fine detail, and their derivatives are SIRENs too. Plotted with ω₀ = 1.

  • [−1, 1]
  • smooth
  • non-monotonic
  • bounded

Sitzmann et al., 2020 (SIREN)

Chosen for Implicit neural representations, Physics-informed neural networks

Cosine

f(x) = cos(x)

Periodic and even. Appears in random Fourier-feature networks and as an alternative to sine in implicit neural representations.

  • [−1, 1]
  • smooth
  • non-monotonic
  • bounded

Sinc

f(x) = sin(x) / x

A decaying oscillation whose Fourier transform is a box: an ideal low-pass filter in function form. Studied as an activation for function approximation.

  • ≈ [−0.22, 1]
  • smooth
  • non-monotonic
  • bounded

Snake

f(x) = x + sin²(ax) / a

The identity plus a periodic ripple, which gives networks an inductive bias toward periodic signals while staying monotonic. BigVGAN uses a version with learnable a for audio synthesis. Plotted with a = 1.

  • (−∞, ∞)
  • smooth
  • monotonic

Ziyin et al., 2020

Chosen for Audio and waveform generation

Growing cosine unit

GCU

f(x) = x · cos(x)

Oscillates with growing amplitude. Because it is non-monotonic with many zeros, a single GCU neuron can learn XOR.

  • (−∞, ∞)
  • smooth
  • non-monotonic

Noel et al., 2021

SinLU

f(x) = (x + a sin(bx)) · σ(x)

A Swish-like gated unit that adds a learned sinusoidal ripple to the input before gating. Plotted with a = b = 1.

  • ≈ [−0.5, ∞)
  • smooth
  • non-monotonic

Paul et al., 2022

Gaussian

RBF

f(x) = e−x²

A bump that responds only near zero. The classic activation of radial basis function networks, and also used in implicit neural representations.

  • (0, 1]
  • smooth
  • non-monotonic
  • bounded

Chosen for Implicit neural representations

  • non-monotonic

f(x) = √(x² + c²)

  • non-monotonic

f(x) = 1 / √(x² + c²)

A heavy-tailed bump: it decays like 1/|x| rather than exponentially, so each unit responds to a wider neighbourhood than a Gaussian (c = 1 plotted).

  • smooth

f(x) = −a + ½ (√((x − a)² + ε) + √((x + a)² + ε))

A smoothed pan function: near zero inside [−a, a], rising linearly outside on both sides.

  • ≈ [0.049, ∞)
  • smooth
  • non-monotonic

Pan et al., 2023 (via Kunc & Kléma, 2024)

BReLUPlus

f(x) = ½ (1 + √(x² + ε) − √((x − 1)² + ε))

A smoothed ReLU capped at 1.

  • ≈ [0, 1]
  • smooth
  • monotonic
  • bounded

Pan et al., 2023 (via Kunc & Kléma, 2024)

SReLUPlus

f(x) = ax + ½(a − 1)(√((x − t)² + ε) − √((x + t)² + ε))

A smoothed symmetric SReLU: slope 1 near zero and slope a beyond ±t.

  • (−∞, ∞)
  • smooth
  • monotonic

Pan et al., 2023 (via Kunc & Kléma, 2024)

HardTanhPlus

f(x) = ½ (√((x + 1)² + ε) − √((x − 1)² + ε))

A smoothed HardTanh with rounded corners at ±1.

  • ≈ [−1, 1]
  • smooth
  • monotonic
  • bounded

Pan et al., 2023 (via Kunc & Kléma, 2024)

HardshrinkPlus

HTFPlus

f(x) = x (1 + ½ ((x − a)/√((x − a)² + ε) − (x + a)/√((x + a)² + ε)))

A smoothed hard-shrink: x multiplied by a smooth window that is near zero inside [−a, a].

  • (−∞, ∞)
  • smooth
  • non-monotonic

Pan et al., 2023 (via Kunc & Kléma, 2024)

ELUPlus

f(x) = ½(x + |x|ε) + ½((ex − 1)/a + |(ex − 1)/a|ε)

The MSRF smoothing applied to ELU's two pieces, as written in the original. Note that, unlike ELU, this form stays positive.

  • ≈ [0.024, ∞)
  • smooth
  • non-monotonic

Pan et al., 2023 (via Kunc & Kléma, 2024)

SwishPlus

f(x) = x · StepPlus(x) = ½ (x + x² / √(x² + ε))

Swish with the sigmoid replaced by the algebraic StepPlus: no exponentials, same overall shape.

  • ≈ [−0.15, ∞)
  • smooth
  • non-monotonic

Pan et al., 2023 (via Kunc & Kléma, 2024)

MishPlus

f(x) = x · BipolarPlus(BipolarPlus(x))

An algebraic Mish-like function built from nested BipolarPlus terms, as written in the original.

  • ≈ [0, ∞)
  • smooth
  • non-monotonic

Pan et al., 2023 (via Kunc & Kléma, 2024)

LogishPlus

f(x) = x · ln(1 + StepPlus(x))

Logish with the sigmoid replaced by StepPlus.

  • ≈ [−0.14, ∞)
  • smooth
  • non-monotonic

Pan et al., 2023 (via Kunc & Kléma, 2024)

SoftsignPlus

f(x) = x / (1 + √(x² + ε))

A softsign whose |x| is mollified, making it smooth at zero. With ε = 1 it coincides with rootsig.

  • ≈ [−1, 1]
  • smooth
  • monotonic
  • bounded

Pan et al., 2023 (via Kunc & Kléma, 2024)

SignReLUPlus

f(x) = ½(x + |x|ε) + (x − |x|ε) / (2|1 − x|ε)

A smoothed approximation of SignReLU (DLU): ReLU-like for positive inputs and a softsign-like dip for negative ones.

  • ≈ [−1, ∞)
  • smooth
  • monotonic

Pan et al., 2023 (via Kunc & Kléma, 2024)

Other research functions

4

One-off proposals and specialised activations that are worth knowing about.

Bent identity

f(x) = (√(x² + 1) − 1) / 2 + x

Almost linear with a gentle bend: the slope goes from 0.5 for large negative inputs to 1.5 for large positive ones. Smooth, monotonic and unbounded.

  • (−∞, ∞)
  • smooth
  • monotonic

SQNL

f(x) =1if x > 2x − x²/4if 0 ≤ x ≤ 2x + x²/4if −2 ≤ x < 0−1if x < −2

Square nonlinearity: a tanh-shaped curve built from two quadratic pieces, cheap enough for hardware without exponential units.

  • [−1, 1]
  • smooth
  • monotonic
  • bounded

Wuraola & Patel, 2018

Penalised tanh

f(x) =tanh(x)if x > 0a · tanh(x)if x ≤ 0

Tanh with the negative side scaled down (a = 0.25), the saturating analogue of a leaky ReLU. A broad NLP comparison later found it unusually stable across tasks.

  • (−a, 1)
  • non-smooth
  • monotonic
  • bounded

Xu et al., 2016; Eger et al., 2018

Cube

f(x) = x³

Used in a neural dependency parser to model three-way interactions between word, part-of-speech and label features directly. Unbounded and fast-growing, so it needs careful scaling.

  • (−∞, ∞)
  • smooth
  • monotonic

Chen & Manning, 2014

No function matches those filters.

In the survey, not drawn here

Most functions come from the survey by Kunc & Kléma (2024), which collects about 400 activation functions. These 52 entries from it have no card because they can't be drawn as one fixed curve of one input:

FunctionWhy it isn't plotted

DualReLUtakes two inputs

How to read a card

The plot

The solid line is the function and the dashed line is its derivative, computed numerically from the same formula. The x-range is printed in the corner; the y-axis is scaled to fit and clipped at ±6. Where a function has parameters, the card plots the stated defaults or several values (see the legend). Vector functions such as softmax are plotted for two classes, and gated units with both inputs tied to x.

The tags

Smooth means differentiable everywhere (no kinks). Monotonic means never decreasing (or never increasing). Bounded means the output stays in a finite interval in both directions. A torch.nn tag means PyTorch ships it as a module. Chosen for links to the use cases where it's a typical pick.

Sources

Each card names the paper usually credited with the function. Cards marked "via Kunc & Kléma, 2024" were collected from the survey Three Decades of Activations: every one of their implementations was checked numerically against the survey's own formula. Where the survey's formula has an evident typo, the card says how it was corrected. Descriptions are our own.

About

The Nonlinearity Index is a growing catalogue of activation functions for deep learning: the formula, how each curve behaves, and a plot of it and its derivative, organised by family and paired with a guide to which functions get chosen for which tasks. It is built as part of the open ActivationFWorks project and grows in batches toward ≈400 functions.

Corrections to formulas, citations or use-case claims are welcome: open an issue or pull request on GitHub.
